title: Adapter and Bridge
scopeHtml: Scope: Adapter (object vs class), Bridge, class diagrams, before/after refactors, when not to use, JDK/Retrofit/JDBC examples.

notes.title: Why structural patterns exist
notes.html:
Structural patterns are about how classes and objects are glued together into bigger structures. Creational patterns answer "how do I make it", behavioral ones answer "how do they talk", structural ones answer "how are the pieces shaped and connected". The seven you must know: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy.

The common trick behind all of them: instead of changing a class, you put another object next to it or around it and use composition (holding a reference) instead of inheritance. Composition can be swapped at runtime; inheritance is frozen at compile time.

Worked example. A payments app has 3 gateways (Stripe, Razorpay, PayPal) and 2 channels (web, mobile). With inheritance you would write 3 x 2 = 6 classes; with composition 3 + 2 = 5, and a fourth gateway costs 1 class, not 2. That arithmetic is the whole argument for Bridge.

Industry examples. Java IO (BufferedInputStream wraps FileInputStream), Android RecyclerView.Adapter, OkHttp interceptors, Retrofit's generated API objects, Servlet filters: all structural patterns in everyday libraries.

Everyday analogy. Travel plug adapters, a gift wrapped in paper, a folder inside a folder: you do not rebuild the thing, you add a shape around it.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming a pattern without saying what problem it solves.
  • Confusing Adapter, Decorator, Proxy: all three wrap one object. The difference is intent (see the comparison file).
  • Forgetting that "prefer composition over inheritance" is the underlying principle.

notes.title: Adapter: the idea
notes.html:
An Adapter makes an existing class fit an interface the client expects, without changing either side. You own the client, you do not own (or do not want to touch) the library. The adapter translates calls.

Mechanism: the adapter implements the target interface and holds the adaptee. Each target method calls the adaptee's method(s), converting arguments and results.

+-----------+      uses      +-----------------+
|  Client   | -------------> | <<Target>>      |
+-----------+                | + pay(rupees)   |
                             +--------+--------+
                                      ^
                                      | implements
                             +--------+--------+      has-a      +------------------+
                             | StripeAdapter   | -------------->  | StripeSdk        |
                             | - sdk           |                  | + charge(cents,  |
                             | + pay(rupees)   |                  |    currency)     |
                             +-----------------+                  +------------------+

Worked example. Your app calls pay(499.0) in rupees. The Stripe SDK wants charge(long amountInMinorUnits, String currency). The adapter does sdk.charge(Math.round(499.0 * 100), "inr") so 49,900 paise reach Stripe. One bug here (using 499 instead of 49,900) means customers pay 1 percent of the price, which is why this conversion lives in exactly one class.

Industry examples. Arrays.asList(array) adapts an array to the List interface. InputStreamReader adapts a byte stream (InputStream) to a character stream (Reader). Android RecyclerView.Adapter adapts your data list to views. Retrofit CallAdapter turns a Call<T> into Single<T>, Flow or a coroutine.

Everyday analogy. A travel plug adapter: the wall socket and your laptop charger are both fine, they just disagree on shape.

Decision gravity. Cheap and reversible: an adapter is a small class and removing it later is a local change. It becomes a one-way door only if the adapter's interface leaks library types everywhere.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the adapter "changes" the adaptee. It never does.
  • Putting business logic in the adapter; it should only translate.
  • Not mentioning Adapter is the standard shield against vendor lock-in.

notes.title: Adapter in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before (no pattern). Every call site talks to the vendor SDK directly. Swapping vendors means editing 40 files.

// BEFORE: SDK types and cents conversion leak into business code
class CheckoutService {
    private final StripeSdk stripe = new StripeSdk();
    void checkout(double rupees) {
        stripe.charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr"); // repeated in every caller
    }
}

After (object adapter).

interface PaymentGateway { boolean pay(double rupees); }

class StripeSdk {                              // third-party, cannot edit
    boolean charge(long minorUnits, String currency) { return minorUnits > 0; }
}

class StripeAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final StripeSdk sdk;
    StripeAdapter(StripeSdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }
    @Override public boolean pay(double rupees) {
        return sdk.charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr");
    }
}

class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;          // depends on the abstraction
    CheckoutService(PaymentGateway g) { this.gateway = g; }
    void checkout(double rupees) { gateway.pay(rupees); }
}

Kotlin variant, plus an extension-function alternative:

interface PaymentGateway { fun pay(rupees: Double): Boolean }

class StripeAdapter(private val sdk: StripeSdk) : PaymentGateway {
    override fun pay(rupees: Double) = sdk.charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr")
}

// Kotlin shortcut: delegation lets you adapt and reuse the rest for free
class LoggingGateway(inner: PaymentGateway) : PaymentGateway by inner

Object vs class adapter. Object adapter (above) uses composition, works in Java and Kotlin, and can adapt subclasses of the adaptee. Class adapter extends the adaptee and implements the target; it needs multiple inheritance, so in Java it works only if the target is an interface. Prefer the object adapter.

Common interview traps.

  • Writing a class adapter and then being unable to explain why it breaks when the adaptee is final.
  • Mixing up the direction: the adapter implements the interface the CLIENT wants, not the library's.

notes.title: Adapter: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not adapt when you own both sides and can simply change one. An adapter between two of your own classes is a sign the design drifted; fix the interface instead.

Skip it when the two interfaces are already nearly identical (one method rename). A thin adapter that only renames is noise, and each extra layer adds a stack frame and a place for bugs.

Do not let it grow into a god translator that also validates, retries and logs. That is Facade or Decorator work.

Worked example. A team wrapped Retrofit in ApiAdapter, wrapped by ApiService, wrapped by ApiRepository, all with the same method names. 3 layers, 0 translation, +1 file to touch per new endpoint (about 15 minutes lost per endpoint across a year of 80 endpoints = 20 hours).

Common interview traps.

  • "Always wrap third-party libraries." Wrap the ones likely to change or leak types; wrapping String helpers is silly.
  • Not noticing a 1:1 wrapper adds no value.

notes.title: Bridge: the idea
notes.html:
Bridge splits one class hierarchy into two independent ones, an abstraction and an implementation, linked by composition so each can vary alone. It prevents the "class explosion" of 2 dimensions of variation.

Mechanism: the abstraction holds a reference to an implementor interface. Subclasses of the abstraction add higher-level behavior; subclasses of the implementor supply low-level operations.

 Abstraction side                       Implementor side
+------------------+   has-a   +---------------------+
| Notification     | --------> | <<MessageSender>>   |
| + send(text)     |           | + deliver(text)     |
+--------+---------+           +----------+----------+
         ^                                ^
   +-----+------+                  +------+-------+------+
   |            |                  |              |      |
 Urgent     Digest             SmsSender   EmailSender  PushSender

Worked example. 3 notification types (Urgent, Digest, Marketing) x 4 channels (SMS, Email, Push, WhatsApp) = 12 classes with inheritance. With Bridge: 3 + 4 = 7. Add a 5th channel: +1 class, not +3. At 10 types x 10 channels the numbers are 100 vs 20.

Industry examples. JDBC: DriverManager/Connection is the abstraction, each database vendor's driver is an implementor. Android's View draws through a Canvas abstraction with different backends (software vs hardware). SLF4J is a facade-plus-bridge: your code uses the SLF4J API, bindings choose Logback or Log4j (treat the exact classification as a discussion point, it is both).

Everyday analogy. A TV remote (abstraction: basic remote, smart remote) and the TV brand (implementor: Sony, Samsung). You can upgrade the remote without changing the TV and vice versa.

Decision gravity. Costs more up front than Adapter. It is a design-time decision, so retrofitting is a refactor (moderately reversible). Worth it only when you truly see two axes growing.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up Bridge and Adapter: Adapter fixes a mismatch AFTER the fact; Bridge is planned UP FRONT to keep two axes separate.
  • Calling every interface-with-implementations a Bridge. Bridge needs two hierarchies.

notes.title: Bridge in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before. Inheritance explosion:

// BEFORE: one class per combination
class UrgentSmsNotification {}
class UrgentEmailNotification {}
class DigestSmsNotification {}
class DigestEmailNotification {}
// ... 12 classes, copy-pasted delivery code

After.

interface MessageSender { void deliver(String to, String body); }
class SmsSender implements MessageSender {
    public void deliver(String to, String body) { System.out.println("SMS " + to + ": " + body); }
}
class EmailSender implements MessageSender {
    public void deliver(String to, String body) { System.out.println("MAIL " + to + ": " + body); }
}

abstract class Notification {
    protected final MessageSender sender;          // the bridge
    Notification(MessageSender s) { this.sender = s; }
    abstract void notifyUser(String user, String text);
}
class UrgentNotification extends Notification {
    UrgentNotification(MessageSender s) { super(s); }
    void notifyUser(String u, String t) { sender.deliver(u, "[URGENT] " + t); }
}
class DigestNotification extends Notification {
    DigestNotification(MessageSender s) { super(s); }
    void notifyUser(String u, String t) { sender.deliver(u, "Daily digest: " + t); }
}

// new UrgentNotification(new SmsSender()).notifyUser("+91-98...", "Server down");
fun interface MessageSender { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) }

abstract class Notification(protected val sender: MessageSender) {
    abstract fun notifyUser(user: String, text: String)
}
class UrgentNotification(s: MessageSender) : Notification(s) {
    override fun notifyUser(user: String, text: String) = sender.deliver(user, "[URGENT] $text")
}
// Kotlin: a SAM lambda is a sender
val sms = MessageSender { to, body -> println("SMS $to: $body") }

Common interview traps.

  • Using inheritance in the abstraction side only and forgetting that the implementor must be injected (constructor), otherwise you cannot swap at runtime.
  • Not being able to produce the class-count arithmetic when asked "why".

notes.title: Bridge: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not use it when there is only one axis of variation. One axis is plain Strategy or an interface, with no second hierarchy to bridge.

Do not use it when the second axis will never grow (for example "we will only ever send email"). You pay indirection for nothing.

It is easy to over-apply to small apps; two classes and an if are fine until the third combination appears.

Worked example. A report exporter with 1 report type and 3 formats is just Strategy (3 + 1 classes). Add a second report dimension (PDF vs dashboard layout) with 4 more formats, and now Bridge pays: 2 + 4 = 6 instead of 8.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing Bridge when Strategy is enough; both use composition, but Bridge has a hierarchy on each side.
  • Forgetting that Bridge is about structure, Strategy is about swapping an algorithm.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Structural patterns glue objects by composition: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy.
  • Adapter translates an existing class to the interface the client wants; use an object adapter; keep it logic-free; do not wrap what you own.
  • Real examples: Arrays.asList, InputStreamReader, RecyclerView.Adapter, Retrofit CallAdapter.
  • Bridge separates two axes (abstraction x implementation) so classes grow as A + B, not A x B.
  • Real examples: JDBC drivers, View/Canvas, logging bindings.
  • Adapter fixes mismatch afterwards; Bridge prevents it up front.
  • Avoid both when there is no real mismatch or only one axis of variation.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Adapter pattern, and what problem does it solve? Give a real example from the JDK or Android.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who can name the pattern from people who can say which side owns the interface and why the wrapper exists.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Adapter makes a class I cannot or do not want to change fit the interface my client already expects. The adapter implements the target interface, holds the adaptee, and translates each call. It never changes the adaptee. InputStreamReader is one: it adapts a byte InputStream to the character Reader interface.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three roles: the Target (interface the client wants), the Adaptee (existing class with a different API), the Adapter (implements Target, has-a Adaptee). The client depends only on Target, so replacing the adaptee means writing one new adapter, not editing every call site.

Client -> <<PaymentGateway>> pay(rupees)
              ^ implements
          StripeAdapter --has-a--> StripeSdk.charge(minorUnits, currency)

Other real ones: Arrays.asList (array to List), RecyclerView.Adapter (data to views), Retrofit CallAdapter (Call<T> to Flow or Single). The adapter is also the usual shield against vendor lock-in: SDK types stop at its boundary.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface PaymentGateway { boolean pay(double rupees); }

class StripeAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final StripeSdk sdk;
    StripeAdapter(StripeSdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }
    public boolean pay(double rupees) { return sdk.charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr"); }
}
interface PaymentGateway { fun pay(rupees: Double): Boolean }

class StripeAdapter(private val sdk: StripeSdk) : PaymentGateway {
    override fun pay(rupees: Double) = sdk.charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the adapter modifies the adaptee.
  • Putting business rules in the adapter; it should only translate.
  • Getting the direction wrong: the adapter implements the interface the client wants, not the library's.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Adapter vs Facade? -> Adapter converts one interface to an expected one; Facade builds a new simpler interface over many classes.
  2. Who creates the adapter? -> The composition root or a DI module, so the client never sees the SDK.
  3. Where should the rupee-to-paise conversion live? -> Only in the adapter, so a unit mistake cannot be repeated in 40 call sites.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives the plug-adapter analogy. Senior names the three roles, says the adapter is the vendor-lock-in boundary, and says what it must not contain (retries, validation, business logic).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that scattered stripe.charge(...) across 40 files needed a two-week migration when the vendor changed; the teams with one adapter changed one class.

questions.contextHtml:
Checkout charges through a Stripe adapter. Finance reports that some orders are short by 1 paisa; for example a Rs 19.99 order settled as Rs 19.98. About 3% of orders are affected. Unit tests only used round prices such as 499.0.

class StripeAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final StripeSdk sdk;
    StripeAdapter(StripeSdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }
    public boolean pay(double rupees) {
        return sdk.charge((long) (rupees * 100), "inr");
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, fix it, and say what you would change in the adapter's contract.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, maybe Stripe rounds wrongly." It blames the vendor and never inspects the cast.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which amounts are off (only values with paise)? Is the target interface in double rupees by design? Do refunds use the same path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship the one-line fix and list the affected orders for finance to reconcile; no feature flag needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) floating-point truncation in the cast; (b) vendor rounding; (c) currency mismatch.
  4. How I'd verify each: In a REPL (long)(19.99 * 100) gives 1998 because 19.99 * 100 is 1998.9999999999998. That confirms (a); (b) and (c) would not depend on the amount's fractional part.
  5. Root cause: (long) truncates toward zero, and a double cannot represent 19.99 exactly.
  6. Fix: short-term Math.round(rupees * 100). Long-term change the Target to take long paise or BigDecimal, so the adapter does not convert from a binary float at all.
  7. Prevention: a property-style test looping over every value 0.00 to 999.99 in paise; ban double for money in review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not scatter rounding fixes in callers; the whole point of the adapter is that conversion lives in one class.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the target is changed to long paise? -> Adapter passes it straight through; the conversion bug class disappears.
  • Zero-decimal currencies like JPY? -> Minor-unit factor is per currency; look it up from the currency, do not hardcode 100 (verify with the vendor docs).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a billing team: a truncation cast shorted merchants 1 paisa on a few percent of orders for six weeks. It was found only when reconciliation totals drifted.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the vendor.
  • Hire: spots the truncation and uses Math.round.
  • Strong hire: also moves money to integer minor units in the Target contract and adds an exhaustive test.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between an object adapter and a class adapter, and which do you choose in Java and Kotlin?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests composition vs inheritance judgement and whether you know language limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An object adapter holds the adaptee as a field (composition). A class adapter extends the adaptee and implements the target. I use the object adapter almost always: it works with a final adaptee, can wrap subclasses of the adaptee, and does not expose the adaptee's methods to my client.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Class adapter needs multiple inheritance in classic form. In Java it only works if the target is an interface and the adaptee is a non-final class. It also inherits all adaptee public methods, so the client can call them through the adapter and the adapter becomes coupled to the adaptee's internals. Object adapter has an extra field and one delegation hop (negligible, the JIT inlines it).

Object adapter: Adapter --has-a--> Adaptee
Class adapter : Adapter --is-a---> Adaptee, implements Target

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

// class adapter: only possible because PaymentGateway is an interface and StripeSdk is not final
class StripeClassAdapter extends StripeSdk implements PaymentGateway {
    public boolean pay(double rupees) { return charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr"); }
}
// Kotlin classes are final by default, so a class adapter needs `open class StripeSdk`
class StripeClassAdapter : StripeSdk(), PaymentGateway {
    override fun pay(rupees: Double) = charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Class adapter on a final adaptee (every Kotlin class unless open); it will not compile.
  • Letting the client see inherited vendor methods, defeating the isolation.
  • Forgetting that the object adapter can wrap a mock subclass of the adaptee in tests.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Kotlin awkward for class adapters? -> Classes are final by default, and third-party ones usually are not open.
  2. Can an object adapter adapt several adaptees? -> Yes, hold several fields; a class adapter cannot extend several classes.
  3. Two-way adapter? -> Implements both interfaces so two worlds can use it; rare, and it is a sign to unify the APIs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites "composition vs inheritance". Senior adds the final-class limit, leaked methods, and that Kotlin by delegation makes the object adapter nearly free.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A class adapter over a vendor client broke when the vendor made the class final in a minor release; the object-adapter teams did not notice.

questions.contextHtml:
Your app uses PaymentGateway with StripeAdapter. Product now wants Razorpay for Indian cards and PayPal for international ones, chosen per order. Razorpay SDK: createOrder(int paise) then capture(String orderId). PayPal SDK: execute(PayPalRequest) where the amount is a String in major units like "19.99". The current code is:

class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    CheckoutService(PaymentGateway g) { gateway = g; }
    boolean checkout(double rupees) { return gateway.pay(rupees); }
}
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, which do not, and where does the per-order choice go?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds if (country == IN) ... else ... into CheckoutService with both SDKs imported. That breaks open/closed and spreads SDK types again.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the choice depend on card country or user? Is fallback between vendors wanted? Same currency semantics on both? Are refunds in scope?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is planned work, so I would keep CheckoutService untouched.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Not applicable; the design question is where variation lives.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add RazorpayAdapter and PayPalAdapter, each implementing PaymentGateway; contract-test all three against the same interface test suite.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable. The principle is that new vendors add classes and do not edit CheckoutService.
  6. Fix: RazorpayAdapter does createOrder(paise) then capture(id) inside pay, hiding the two-step flow. PayPalAdapter formats BigDecimal.valueOf(rupees).setScale(2).toPlainString(). Per-order choice goes in a small GatewayRouter implements PaymentGateway (or a factory) chosen at the composition root, so CheckoutService still sees one interface.
  7. Prevention: a shared abstract contract test (pay(10.00) true, pay(0) false) run against every adapter; an architecture test that only adapter packages import SDKs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not push vendor-specific options into PaymentGateway; if a vendor needs extras, the interface is too thin and I would extend it deliberately, not leak.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Razorpay needs a webhook, the others do not? -> The webhook is outside pay; model it as a separate inbound adapter, not a bloated one.
  • Router with fallback on vendor outage? -> A Decorator or Router that catches and tries the next gateway, but only for idempotent calls with an idempotency key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team added the third vendor by pasting else if into checkout; two years later each vendor change meant editing a 900-line method. Their rewrite was the same three adapters they had skipped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds if branches in checkout.
  • Hire: one adapter per vendor behind the existing interface.
  • Strong hire: adds router at the composition root, contract tests, and handles the two-step Razorpay flow and idempotency.

questions.contextHtml:
In code review you see this for a feature that has 80 endpoints:

class ApiService(private val retrofit: UserApi) {            // same method names as UserApi
    suspend fun getUser(id: String) = retrofit.getUser(id)
}
class ApiAdapter(private val service: ApiService) {          // same again
    suspend fun getUser(id: String) = service.getUser(id)
}
class ApiRepository(private val adapter: ApiAdapter) {      // same again
    suspend fun getUser(id: String) = adapter.getUser(id)
}

Each new endpoint needs 4 edits. Estimated 15 minutes per endpoint of boilerplate.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, what do you tell the author, and when would an adapter layer be justified here?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It is layered architecture, looks clean." Layers with zero translation are noise.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does any layer convert types (DTO to domain), handle errors, or hide Retrofit? Is a second backend planned? Are there tests at each layer?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not block the PR on a rewrite; ask for the two redundant layers to be removed before more endpoints are added.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) cargo-cult layering; (b) a past requirement that no longer exists; (c) intent to isolate Retrofit that was never finished.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read git history for why they exist, grep for anything but pass-through code, check whether DTO types leak past the repository.
  5. Root cause: Adapters are for interface mismatch. Here the interfaces are identical so there is nothing to adapt.
  6. Fix: Keep one boundary: the repository maps UserDto to User and maps errors to domain results. Delete ApiService and ApiAdapter. 80 endpoints x 15 minutes is about 20 hours a year saved.
  7. Prevention: a review rule: every layer must add translation, policy or a seam someone uses; "same name, same signature" is a delete.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not wrap everything for "future flexibility". I do keep one wrapper where the vendor type would otherwise leak into the domain.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• But we may swap Retrofit someday. -> Then the repository is the seam; one boundary covers it, three do not help more.
  • Wrapper makes mocking easier? -> Retrofit interfaces are already mockable; interface plus fake is enough.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a codebase with four same-named layers, where a new field meant touching nine files and a typo was found in the third pass-through only after release.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts all layers.
  • Hire: removes pass-through layers and keeps one mapping boundary.
  • Strong hire: gives the rule for when a layer is justified and quantifies the cost.

questions.contextHtml:
CheckoutService is written like this and the team cannot unit test it without a Stripe sandbox key; the CI job takes 90 seconds and fails 1 run in 20 on network flakes.

class CheckoutService {
    private final StripeSdk stripe = new StripeSdk("sk_test_...");
    boolean checkout(double rupees) {
        if (rupees <= 0) return false;
        return stripe.charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr");
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: How do you restructure it so the business logic is testable in milliseconds, and how do you still test the Stripe translation?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Mockito to mock the new StripeSdk()" (needs static or constructor mocking) or "mark the test as integration and live with it".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the SDK class final? Any other callers? Is DI already in use?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Skip the flaky test in the PR gate and run it nightly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Not a debugging problem; the cause is a hard-wired dependency.
  4. How I'd verify each: After the refactor, run the service test with no network: it must pass offline.
  5. Root cause: new StripeSdk inside the class means no seam; the business rule (rupees <= 0) is tied to the network.
  6. Fix: Extract PaymentGateway, inject it, and write StripeAdapter. Tests use a fake.
  7. Prevention: adapters get a thin test against a fake SDK object (check 19.99 gives 1999 paise), plus one nightly sandbox test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not mock the vendor SDK in every business test; the interface I own is the seam.
interface PaymentGateway { boolean pay(double rupees); }

class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    CheckoutService(PaymentGateway g) { gateway = g; }
    boolean checkout(double rupees) { return rupees > 0 && gateway.pay(rupees); }
}

// test: no network, runs in microseconds
class CheckoutServiceTest {
    void rejectsZero() {
        boolean[] called = {false};
        CheckoutService s = new CheckoutService(r -> { called[0] = true; return true; });
        assert !s.checkout(0) && !called[0];
    }
}
interface PaymentGateway { fun pay(rupees: Double): Boolean }

class CheckoutService(private val gateway: PaymentGateway) {
    fun checkout(rupees: Double) = rupees > 0 && gateway.pay(rupees)
}
// test: CheckoutService { true }.checkout(0) must be false

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fake vs mock? -> A fake that records calls is simpler and survives refactors; use mock verification only for "was it called".
  • How do you keep the adapter honest? -> One contract test run against fake and real sandbox.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the 90-second flaky payment tests were skipped in CI "temporarily" for a year; a refactor then broke zero-amount handling and nobody noticed until prod.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: static mocking tricks or leaves it.
  • Hire: extracts the interface and injects it.
  • Strong hire: separates logic tests, adapter translation tests and one sandbox test, with the reason for each.

questions.promptHtml: Bridge and Strategy both use composition and an injected interface. How do you tell them apart, and when is Strategy enough?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates over-apply Bridge. The signal is whether you count axes of variation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Strategy swaps one algorithm behind one interface: one axis. Bridge splits a class hierarchy into two hierarchies, abstraction and implementor, because both vary independently. If I have one thing that changes, it is Strategy; if I have two dimensions that would multiply classes, it is Bridge.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strategy: context holds a Strategy; implementations differ in how they compute. Bridge: Notification (Urgent, Digest, Marketing) holds a MessageSender (Sms, Email, Push). Both sides have subclasses and both can grow. The test is arithmetic: with A abstractions and B implementors, inheritance needs A x B classes, Bridge needs A + B. At 3 x 4 that is 12 vs 7; at 10 x 10 it is 100 vs 20. One report type with 3 formats is Strategy: 3 + 1 classes; a Bridge there is ceremony.

Strategy: Context --has-a--> Strategy {A, B, C}
Bridge  : Abstraction {X, Y} --has-a--> Implementor {A, B, C}

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

// Strategy: one axis
class Exporter { private final Format f; Exporter(Format f) { this.f = f; } String run(Report r) { return f.render(r); } }
// Strategy in Kotlin can be just a function type
class Exporter(private val render: (Report) -> String) { fun run(r: Report) = render(r) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling every interface with several implementations a Bridge.
  • Building a second hierarchy that has exactly one subclass.
  • Claiming the difference is the diagram; the shapes are identical, the intent and the second hierarchy differ.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a Bridge be refactored from Strategy later? -> Yes, when a second axis appears; start with Strategy.
  2. Which one is a runtime swap? -> Both; Bridge's implementor is usually fixed at construction.
  3. Is JDBC a Bridge? -> Roughly: Connection API (abstraction) over vendor drivers (implementors); treat the exact classification as a discussion.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "they are the same with different names". Senior counts axes, shows the class arithmetic, and defaults to the cheaper one.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reporting module shipped a Bridge for one report type; two years on nobody could explain the second hierarchy that had one subclass.

questions.contextHtml:
A notification module has grown by copy-paste:

class UrgentSmsNotification { void notifyUser(String u, String t) { /* sms http call */ } }
class UrgentEmailNotification { void notifyUser(String u, String t) { /* smtp call */ } }
class DigestSmsNotification { /* same sms code again */ }
class DigestEmailNotification { /* same smtp code again */ }
// ... 3 types x 4 channels = 12 classes today

Product wants WhatsApp next quarter, and a "Marketing" type after. Each channel's HTTP code is already duplicated 3 times and two copies have diverged (one has a timeout, others do not).
questions.promptHtml: Refactor it. Which pattern, which classes, and how many classes do you have before and after the two requests?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make a base class with a template method." That keeps the cross product and the duplicated delivery code.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does a notification type ever depend on a channel capability (HTML only on email)? Fixed channel per type or chosen per user? Are more channels or more types expected?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the missing timeout in the divergent copies first; it is a live risk.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two orthogonal axes (what we say: type; how we deliver: channel). Alternative: one axis only, if types never vary behavior; checked from the code, they only prefix the text.
  4. How I'd verify each: Diff the 12 classes; if differences per row are only prefix text and per column only delivery code, the axes are orthogonal.
  5. Root cause: Inheritance encodes both dimensions in one hierarchy.
  6. Fix: Bridge: MessageSender implementors (Sms, Email, Push, later WhatsApp) and Notification abstraction subclasses (Urgent, Digest, later Marketing), joined by constructor injection. Before: 12 classes. After: 7 today, and with WhatsApp plus Marketing 5 + 4 = 9 against 20 under inheritance.
  7. Prevention: a contract test on every MessageSender (timeout, empty recipient), and a review rule against XYZ + ABC + Notification name combinations.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make senders know notification types. Cost: one more indirection and a constructor that needs wiring.
interface MessageSender { void deliver(String to, String body); }
abstract class Notification {
    protected final MessageSender sender;
    Notification(MessageSender s) { sender = s; }
    abstract void notifyUser(String user, String text);
}
class UrgentNotification extends Notification {
    UrgentNotification(MessageSender s) { super(s); }
    void notifyUser(String u, String t) { sender.deliver(u, "[URGENT] " + t); }
}
fun interface MessageSender { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) }
abstract class Notification(protected val sender: MessageSender) { abstract fun notifyUser(user: String, text: String) }
class UrgentNotification(s: MessageSender) : Notification(s) {
    override fun notifyUser(user: String, text: String) = sender.deliver(user, "[URGENT] $text")
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Marketing must send only on channels the user opted into. -> That is policy on the abstraction side (filter the sender list), not a new subclass per channel.
  • Both axes only have 2 values and will never grow? -> Then 4 classes are fine; do not bridge.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team with 20 notification classes needed three days to add one channel; after bridging, the same change took an afternoon.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: template-method base class.
  • Hire: identifies Bridge and gives 12 vs 7 arithmetic.
  • Strong hire: also checks the axes are truly orthogonal, fixes the timeout drift, and adds sender contract tests.

questions.promptHtml: Adapter and Bridge both put an interface between a client and an implementation. What is different in intent, timing and structure, and can they appear together?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Both are structural and look alike. A senior knows that one is a retrofit and the other is upfront design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Adapter is applied after the fact to make two existing, incompatible things work together. Bridge is a design decision made up front to keep two hierarchies, an abstraction and its implementations, independent. They combine well: I bridge my abstraction and write an adapter for each third-party implementor that does not fit my implementor interface.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Timing: Adapter responds to a mismatch you did not create; Bridge prevents a combinatorial hierarchy you would create. Structure: Adapter has one wrapped class and no hierarchy on the client side; Bridge has an abstraction hierarchy that has-a implementor hierarchy. In practice, Notification is the abstraction, MessageSender is the implementor interface, and TwilioSender is an Adapter over the vendor SDK that implements MessageSender.

UrgentNotification --has-a--> MessageSender <|-- TwilioAdapter --has-a--> TwilioSdk
        (Bridge: abstraction side -> implementor side)   (Adapter: fits SDK to implementor)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

class TwilioSender implements MessageSender {          // Adapter on the implementor side
    private final TwilioSdk sdk;
    TwilioSender(TwilioSdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }
    public void deliver(String to, String body) { sdk.sendSms("+91" + to, body, false); }
}
new UrgentNotification(new TwilioSender(sdk)).notifyUser("9876543210", "down");
class TwilioSender(private val sdk: TwilioSdk) : MessageSender {
    override fun deliver(to: String, body: String) { sdk.sendSms("+91$to", body, false) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying Bridge "adapts" the implementor; Bridge defines the implementor interface itself.
  • Applying Bridge to retrofit one mismatched class.
  • Forgetting a second hierarchy is the whole point of Bridge.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who owns the implementor interface in Bridge? -> You do, designed for your abstraction's needs.
  2. Can an Adapter be retrofitted to a Bridge? -> Only by designing the second axis; that is a refactor.
  3. A Facade in the mix? -> Facade may sit above the abstraction as the app's entry point.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Bridge decouples abstraction and implementation". Senior: intent and timing, class arithmetic, and the layering with adapters per vendor.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SMS layer built as Bridge plus per-vendor Adapter let a team move off a vendor in one sprint with zero changes to notification types.

questions.contextHtml:
To support a "switch to backup SMS vendor" button, someone made the bridge mutable. In production at 2,000 notifications/s, after a failover a few messages show a body for one user and the recipient of another, and a stack trace shows an NPE twice a day.

abstract class Notification {
    protected MessageSender sender;                 // swapped by an admin thread
    void setSender(MessageSender s) { this.sender = s; }
    abstract void notifyUser(String user, String text);
}
class UrgentNotification extends Notification {
    private String lastUser;                        // "for logging"
    void notifyUser(String user, String text) {
        lastUser = user;
        sender.deliver(lastUser, "[URGENT] " + text);
    }
}
// one shared UrgentNotification instance is used by all request threads
questions.promptHtml: Name every concurrency defect and propose a safe design that still supports vendor failover.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make notifyUser synchronized." That serializes 2,000/s through one lock and does not address the instance state or the visibility problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is one Notification instance shared by design? Does failover need to be instant, or is "within a second" fine? Can a message be sent twice during failover?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove lastUser (use the parameter) and make sender volatile as a stopgap; hot-fix in minutes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lastUser is shared mutable state, so threads interleave: user A's field is overwritten by B before deliver runs; (b) sender is a plain field, so the swap has no visibility guarantee; (c) the NPE: a half-initialised or null sender during setSender(null) used as "disable".
  4. How I'd verify each: A stress test with 32 threads and distinct users asserting each deliver receives its own user; run with jcstress or a loop that fails within seconds; review for the null assignment.
  5. Root cause: Shared mutable state across threads without synchronization and publication.
  6. Fix: Make notifications immutable and stateless; hold the sender in an AtomicReference<MessageSender> or have a FailoverSender implements MessageSender decorator that owns the swap. The bridge field stays final and failover lives inside the implementor side.
  7. Prevention: lint or review rule against non-final fields on shared singletons, a concurrent test in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a global lock. AtomicReference reads are cheap; a messages in flight finish on the old vendor, which I accept as at-least-once.
class FailoverSender implements MessageSender {
    private final AtomicReference<MessageSender> active;
    FailoverSender(MessageSender primary) { active = new AtomicReference<>(primary); }
    void switchTo(MessageSender s) { active.set(s); }
    public void deliver(String to, String body) { active.get().deliver(to, body); }
}
class FailoverSender(primary: MessageSender) : MessageSender {
    private val active = java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference(primary)
    fun switchTo(s: MessageSender) = active.set(s)
    override fun deliver(to: String, body: String) = active.get().deliver(to, body)
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Failover should happen automatically on errors? -> Circuit breaker around the sender with the same decorator, using idempotency keys to avoid duplicates.
  • Why not synchronized on setSender only? -> Writes become safe, but reads of the field on the hot path still lack visibility without volatile or a lock.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a singleton formatter kept the "current user" in a field; messages crossed users during a traffic spike and became a privacy incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds synchronized and stops.
  • Hire: finds both the shared field and the visibility bug and removes the state.
  • Strong hire: moves failover into the implementor side with an atomic swap and writes a concurrent test.

questions.contextHtml: A report exporter has 1 report type today (Sales) and 3 output formats (CSV, PDF, XLSX). A teammate proposes a Bridge: Report abstraction x Format implementor, with a "future-proof" ReportFactory. Roadmap, honestly: a second report type "maybe next year", formats stable. Team of 4, release every 2 weeks.
questions.promptHtml: Do you accept the Bridge? Show the numbers and what triggers revisiting it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts it because "it is the right pattern for report and format" without counting axes or cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a second report type funded or a guess? Do report types differ in structure or only data? Does each report need format-specific layout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would write down the decision and a trigger.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: One real axis (format) so Strategy; or two axes soon, so Bridge.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count classes: one type with 3 formats is Strategy: 1 + 3 = 4 classes, versus Bridge 1 + 3 plus factory and extra interface. With a second type and 4 more format variants: Bridge 2 + 4 = 6 against 8 by inheritance, so Bridge starts to pay at the second type.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable; it is speculation vs a measurable trigger.
  6. Fix: Use Strategy (Format interface injected into the exporter) now. Decision gravity is low: moving from Strategy to Bridge is a local refactor, a two-way door. Revisit when the second report type is funded.
  7. Prevention: note the trigger in the ADR: "second report type with its own layout".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not build the second hierarchy for a hypothetical. The cost of waiting is a small refactor; the cost of building is permanent indirection.
interface Format { byte[] render(Report r); }
class Exporter {
    private final Format format;
    Exporter(Format f) { format = f; }
    byte[] export(Report r) { return format.render(r); }
}
fun interface Format { fun render(r: Report): ByteArray }
class Exporter(private val format: Format) { fun export(r: Report) = format.render(r) }

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Next quarter a Dashboard report with its own layout ships. -> Now two axes with format-specific layout; refactor to Bridge, about a day, and tests already cover the formats.
  • The CEO says "it will definitely grow". -> Write it as a funded item with a date before bridging.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team prebuilt abstractions for three imagined exporters; two were never built, and onboarding docs spent a page explaining unused seams.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts without analysis.
  • Hire: argues for Strategy with the class count.
  • Strong hire: names the trigger, treats the choice as a reversible decision and records it.

questions.contextHtml:
You review a PR titled "Stripe adapter". The team lead notes the vendor changes its error shape often.

class StripeAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final StripeSdk sdk;
    StripeAdapter(StripeSdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }

    public StripeCharge pay(Order order) throws StripeException {   // returns vendor type
        if (order.getTotal() > order.getUser().getCreditLimit())     // business rule
            throw new IllegalStateException("limit");
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {                                // retry
            try { return sdk.charge(order.getTotal(), "inr"); }
            catch (StripeException e) { Thread.sleep(500); }
        }
        log.info("card " + order.getCardNumber());                  // logging
        return null;
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: List the problems and show the shape you would approve.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Focuses on style and naming, misses that vendor types leak and retries risk double charges.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does Stripe get an idempotency key? Who owns the credit-limit rule? Which callers use StripeCharge?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the merge: the card number in logs is a PCI-relevant leak, and null on failure plus blind retries can double charge.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Author mixed Adapter, Decorator (retry, log) and domain logic into one class.
  4. How I'd verify each: grep callers for StripeCharge and StripeException imports outside the adapter package; check logs for card data.
  5. Root cause: The adapter is a god translator, and its signature leaks the vendor, so the isolation benefit is zero.
  6. Fix: Interface PaymentGateway { PaymentResult pay(Money amount, IdempotencyKey key); } with domain types. The adapter only converts and maps vendor errors to domain errors. The credit limit goes in CheckoutService; retry with idempotency key and backoff goes in a RetryingGateway decorator; logging masks the card.
  7. Prevention: an architecture test that vendor packages are imported only in the adapter; secrets scanning in log statements.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not retry non-idempotent charges. Splitting means three small classes instead of one; acceptable, each is independently testable.
class StripeAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final StripeSdk sdk;
    StripeAdapter(StripeSdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }
    public PaymentResult pay(Money amount, IdempotencyKey key) {
        try {
            sdk.charge(amount.minorUnits(), amount.currency(), key.value());
            return PaymentResult.ok();
        } catch (StripeException e) {
            return PaymentResult.failed(mapReason(e));
        }
    }
}
class StripeAdapter(private val sdk: StripeSdk) : PaymentGateway {
    override fun pay(amount: Money, key: IdempotencyKey): PaymentResult =
        try { sdk.charge(amount.minorUnits, amount.currency, key.value); PaymentResult.Ok }
        catch (e: StripeException) { PaymentResult.Failed(mapReason(e)) }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Vendor changes the exception hierarchy. -> Only mapReason changes.
  • Should the adapter return null on failure? -> No; return a result type so callers cannot forget the failure path.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a retry loop inside an adapter retried a timed-out charge that had succeeded; 31 customers were charged twice before an idempotency key was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: style nits only.
  • Hire: separates retry, logging and domain rule from the adapter and removes the vendor type from the signature.
  • Strong hire: adds idempotency, error mapping, PCI log concern and an architecture test.
